analysis.one_liner: Expands Social Security benefits and funds them with new taxes on high incomes.
analysis.headline: Introduced by Sen. Sanders with 10 Democratic cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise Social Security checks across the board, switch inflation adjustments to an index that tracks what seniors actually buy, create a minimum benefit for people who worked long careers at low wages, and let students of deceased or disabled workers keep benefits until age 22. It would pay for this by applying Social Security payroll taxes to income above $250,000 (today wages above roughly $160,000 are exempt) and by more than quadrupling the tax on investment income, from 3.8% to 16.2%, while extending that tax to active business income. It would also merge the retirement and disability trust funds into one.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future Social Security beneficiaries get a permanent across-the-board increase through a richer benefit formula, with the biggest gains going to lifetime low earners, who would get a new minimum benefit tied to the poverty line if they worked 30 or more years [S2, S3]. Beneficiaries would also see cost-of-living adjustments based on a price index for elderly consumers rather than the general index [S2, S3]. Children of retired, deceased, or disabled workers who stay in school full time could keep collecting until age 22 instead of 19 [S2, S3]. The new taxes on income above $250,000 and on investment gains are directed into the trust fund, which the bill says would secure the program's long-term solvency [S2, S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Social Security beneficiaries and lifetime low earners

how_it_helps.text: Raises every beneficiary's check by changing the benefit formula: the first 90% of average earnings is replaced at 95%, and an additional 22% boost is applied to the calculation, effective for benefits in 2024 and after [S3].

Creates a new minimum benefit for lifetime low earners: someone with 30 or more years of covered work could not receive less than 125% of the annual poverty guideline, scaled up from 6.25% for those with 11 years of work [S3].

Switches the annual cost-of-living adjustment from the standard Consumer Price Index to the Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers, which weights the medical and housing costs seniors actually face [S2, S3].

Lets children of retired, deceased, or disabled workers who are full-time students keep receiving benefits until age 22, instead of losing them at 19, and applies the same change to railroad retirement benefits [S2, S3].

Directs the new revenue from the payroll tax extension and the increased investment income tax into a single Social Security Trust Fund, which the bill's stated purpose is to keep solvent long-term [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: High earners and wealthy investors. Social Security payroll taxes would be extended to wages and self-employment income above $250,000, an amount currently exempt (the 2023 cap was $160,200) [S2, S3]. The net investment income tax would rise from 3.8% to 16.2% and would newly cover active trade or business income, hitting owners of partnerships, S corporations, and other pass-through businesses [S2, S3]. Employers of high earners would owe the matching payroll tax share on wages above the current cap up to $250,000 [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners, investors, and pass-through business owners

drawbacks.text: The tax increases are steep and concentrated: the net investment income tax would rise from 3.8% to 16.2% and extend to active business income, and payroll taxes would reach income between the current wage cap and $250,000, raising costs for high earners, investors, pass-through business owners, and their employers [S2, S3]. Opponents would argue this discourages investment and work at the top.

The record contains no independent cost estimate (no Congressional Budget Office score), so whether the new taxes would actually cover the permanent benefit increases for the long term cannot be verified from the material provided; the solvency claim rests on the bill's own framing [S1, S2].

Switching cost-of-living adjustments to the elderly price index would make benefits grow faster than under the current index indefinitely, a compounding cost an honest supporter would have to weigh against the dedicated new revenue [S2, S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are broad and concrete: larger checks for roughly all beneficiaries, a real poverty floor for lifelong low earners, and better inflation protection, paid for by taxes confined to income above $250,000 and to investment gains. The costs fall on a small, high-income group rather than on beneficiaries or general taxpayers, which is the point of the design. The genuine uncertainties are whether the taxes fully cover the compounding cost of richer benefits and the faster index over decades, and the burden the new rates place on high-income investors and business owners, which opponents would weigh heavily.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never acted on it, so it died quietly when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Bernie Sanders introduced the Social Security Expansion Act on February 13, 2023, joined by ten Democratic senators as original cosponsors, including Elizabeth Warren, Cory Booker, and Kirsten Gillibrand [S1, S3, S4].
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance, which holds jurisdiction over Social Security and tax legislation [S5].
The complete action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor consideration, and no House companion action at any point during the two-year Congress [S5].
With the 118th Congress ending January 3, 2025, the bill expired; under Senate rules any bill not passed by both chambers dies at the end of a Congress and must start over from scratch [S5, S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners, investors, and pass-through business owners are better off because the bill died, since they would have paid the new payroll and investment income taxes. Beneficiaries gained nothing, and Social Security's financing was left unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners and investors who avoided the taxes

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled ten Democratic cosponsors on the day of introduction

for.name: Sens. Warren, Whitehouse, Merkley, Van Hollen, Padilla, Gillibrand, Booker, Smith, and Markey
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction, giving the bill its entire recorded support

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance (Chair Ron Wyden)
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction; chaired by Sen. Ron Wyden (D-OR)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving it with no action for two years

sides.party_line_note: All ten cosponsors were Democrats joining independent Sen. Sanders, no Republicans supported the bill, and because it never reached a vote there is no roll call to measure the split.

industries.note: The net investment income tax would more than quadruple, from 3.8% to 16.2%, on investment gains. Their gain in avoiding this tax came directly at the expense of the larger benefit checks the bill would have funded.

industries.industry: Pass-through business owners (partnerships, S corporations, professional practices)
industries.note: The bill removes the exemption that keeps active trade or business income out of the net investment income tax, so owners of law firms, medical practices, real estate partnerships, and similar businesses would pay the new 16.2% rate on business profits.

Employers would owe the matching 6.2% payroll tax on wages above the current cap up to $250,000 per employee, raising the cost of highly compensated staff, with successor-employer rules included to prevent avoidance through company sales.

industries.industry: Social Security trust funds (as administrative structures)
industries.note: The bill merges the Old-Age and Survivors fund and the Disability fund into a single Social Security Trust Fund and directs all new tax revenue into it, a consolidation that simplifies the program's finances but changes no one's benefits by itself.
